title: Private Deployments: VPC & On-Prem Comprehensive Deployment + Day-2 Ops Guide
author: Maya Thompson
body:
Overview

This document is a consolidated reference for Private Deployments at Redwood Inference: VPC-hosted and on-prem (air-gapped) deployments. It combines reference architectures, on-prem packaging guidance, pre-deployment customer requirements, an operational (day-2) checklist, and tested upgrade & rollback procedures. Intended audience: solutions architects, SREs, and platform engineers who own customer private deployments.

Goals
- Provide a single source-of-truth for repeatable, secure private deployments.
- Surface configuration options, sizing guidance, and automation examples.
- Define day-2 ops SLOs, monitoring, and routine operational procedures.
- Describe safe upgrade and rollback procedures with clear ownership and escalation paths.

Scope
Covers: network/VPC reference architectures, on-prem packaging and install options (Kubernetes/Helm, RKE/OKD, air-gapped bundles), pre-deployment customer requirements library, day-2 ops (monitoring, backups, scaling), and upgrade/rollback playbooks. This doc does not replace customer-specific runbooks; instead it should be referenced when authoring customer runbooks.

1) Quick reference: responsibilities and ownership
- Redwood responsibilities: control-plane components, packaged runtime artifacts, validated release bundles, upgrade/rollback artifacts, deployment automation (Terraform/Helm templates), and security guidance.
- Customer responsibilities: cloud accounts / on-prem hardware, network ACLs/firewall rules, KMS/HSM setup, private registry access, host OS hardening, and backups for customer-managed state (if applicable).
- Owner: eng-private-deployments. SRE oncall (primary) + Solutions Eng (secondary) for initial deployment window.

2) High-level reference architectures
A. VPC (Cloud-hosted private deployment) - Use case: customers who want private control plane but host in their cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure).
- Core components:
  - Control plane (Redwood-managed or customer-managed; usually deployed in a dedicated management VPC)
  - Data plane (model-serving nodes) in customer VPC/subnets
  - Private ECR/Artifact registry access
  - KMS integration (customer-managed)
  - Bastion + administrative jump hosts (restricted via SSM/OS login)
- Recommended network layout (minimal):
  - 3 subnets: control-plane (private), data-plane (private; autoscaling groups/POD subnets), management/bastion (private with controlled egress)
  - Route tables: default deny, explicit NAT/Egress for registry, metrics, and telemetry endpoints
  - Security groups: least-privilege: control-plane -> data-plane on gRPC/HTTP ports; data-plane -> KMS endpoints; bastion -> control-plane admin ports only
- Sizing guidance (example starting point for inference-heavy workloads):
  - Small: 4 x A10G / 8 x A100-v2 (model-mix dependent)
  - Medium: 8 x A100-v2 + 2 management instances (control-plane)
  - Large: 16+ GPUs behind autoscaling with burst pools for peak traffic
- Example Terraform module inputs (snippet):
```hcl
module "redwood_vpc" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.redwood.ai/infra/modules//private-deployments/vpc"
  region = var.region
  cidr_block = "10.10.0.0/16"
  public_subnets = ["10.10.0.0/24"]
  private_subnets = ["10.10.1.0/24","10.10.2.0/24"]
  enable_private_registry = true
}
```

B. On-Prem / Air-gapped (Customer data center)
- Use case: regulated customers with no outbound network or strict egress controls.
- Core components:
  - On-prem Kubernetes cluster (validated distributions: RKE2, EKS-D, OpenShift OKD)
  - Private artifact registry (Harbor/Artifactory) mirrored with curated bundles
  - Optional HSM/KMS appliance or PKCS11-compatible key manager
  - NFS/CSI-backed persistent storage for model cache & metadata
- Network and firewall guidance:
  - Plan for minimal required egress during install (one-time access to Redwood artifact CDN) or use offline bundle delivery.
  - Allow internal ports: control-plane gRPC/HTTP endpoints, data-plane model serving ports, etc.
- Packaging options:
  - Air-gapped bundle (tarball) with Helm charts, container images (OCI layout), and signed release manifest
  - On-prem installer (CLI) that validates pre-reqs and applies manifests
- Example install command (air-gapped):
```bash
# On a jump host with the bundle extracted
./redwood-install.sh --bundle ./redwood-private-bundle-2027.02.0.tgz --kubeconfig /root/.kube/config --namespace redwood
```

3) On-prem packaging & release artifacts
- Release bundle contents:
  - Helm charts (templates + values files)
  - OCI image tarballs or mirrored registry references
  - Signed release manifest (SHA256 checksums)
  - Migration scripts (DB schema / metadata migrations)
  - Post-install validation scripts and smoke tests
- Signing & verification: bundles are PGP-signed; install process verifies signature and checksum before applying.
- Recommended Helm values structure (example snippet):
```yaml
global:
  imageRegistry: "my-registry.local"
  storageClass: "csi-nfs"
controlPlane:
  replicas: 3
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: 2
      memory: 8Gi
dataPlane:
  nodeSelector:
    workload-type: model-serving
  gpu: true
```

4) Customer requirements library (pre-deployment checklist)
Provide this form to customers to collect configuration and constraints. Use as the canonical requirements intake for Solutions Eng.
- Network & Identity
  1) Cloud provider / On-prem distribution and version
  2) VPC CIDR plan and subnet ranges (for cloud deployments)
  3) Allowed outbound endpoints & proxy details (if any)
  4) IAM / service account strategy; role ARNs if AWS
  5) KMS/HSM details and access process
- Compute & Storage
  1) Expected qps and latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99)
  2) Model catalog and peak concurrency per model
  3) GPU SKU preferences (A100, H100, A10G)
  4) Storage performance needs (IOPS, throughput)
- Security & Compliance
  1) Data residency/retention requirements
  2) Network segmentation / PCI/HIPAA controls needed
  3) Audit log retention policy and SIEM forwarder details
- Operations & Support
  1) Oncall contacts and escalation matrix
  2) Backup windows and RPO/RTO targets
  3) Maintenance windows and blackout periods
- Delivery options
  1) Access method for image bundles (S3 presigned / VPN / physical transfer)
  2) Preferred automation (Terraform + Helm / manual)
  3) Acceptance criteria and smoke tests for handover

5) Deployment checklist (canonical procedure)
Pre-deploy (validation & provisioning):
1. Verify customer requirements intake is complete and signed off.
2. Confirm network connectivity and firewall rules (test connectivity to registry, KMS endpoints if cloud).
3. Provision management VPC or on-prem management network; create necessary service accounts and IAM roles.
4. Validate Kubernetes cluster (version/CRDs/cni) and node labeling strategy (GPU nodes tainted/labeled).
5. Push images to customer registry or verify mirror.
6. Prepare secrets: TLS certs, KMS credentials, registry credentials, license keys.

Deploy (day 0):
1. Apply namespace + RBAC: kubectl apply -f namespaces-and-rbac.yaml
2. Install control-plane Helm chart: helm upgrade --install redwood-control ./charts/control-plane -f values-control.yaml
3. Wait for control-plane readiness: kubectl rollout status deployment/redwood-control --namespace redwood --timeout=10m
4. Install data-plane and model-serving components: helm upgrade --install redwood-data ./charts/data-plane -f values-data.yaml
5. Run smoke tests: ./smoke-test.sh --endpoint https://redwood-api.local --apikey ${API_KEY}

Post-deploy:
1. Verify telemetry and logs are forwarding to configured observability endpoints (Prometheus, Loki, Grafana).
2. Run load test at 20% of expected traffic to validate autoscaling and batching behavior.
3. Confirm backup snapshot schedule for metadata DB and model cache (if required).
4. Handover runbook and run a knowledge transfer session with customer operators.

6) Day-2 operations (SLOs, monitoring, common procedures)
SLO targets (typical):
- Request latency (text generation) p50 < 50ms, p95 < 250ms, p99 < 600ms for small models; targets should be tuned per-customer SLA.
- Availability: 99.9% monthly for control-plane endpoints.
- Job queue processing: backlogged items processed within 10 minutes at normal load.

Monitoring & alerting (baseline):
- Metrics: request_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), gpu_utilization, batch_size_histogram, kv_cache_hit_rate, queue_depth.
- Alerts (examples):
  - P1: control-plane API 5xx rate > 2% for 5m
  - P1: data-plane node down (GPU node not Ready)
  - P2: queue_depth > threshold for 15m
  - P2: kv_cache_hit_rate < 30% sustained for 10m
- Dashboards: per-model latency breakdown, cost-per-token, autoscaler activity, GPU utilization heatmap.

Routine ops playbook (examples):
- Scaling: adjust node pool size or autoscaling target; prefer vertical burst pools for short-term spikes.
- Cache warmup: after an upgrade, warm model KV caches by running the canonical warmup prompt set (stored in /deploy/smoke/warmup-prompts.json).
- Backups: nightly DB dump to customer-managed S3/BR storage with retention policy defined in intake form.

7) Upgrade and rollback procedures
Principles: upgrades must be staged (canary or blue/green), with explicit pre-checks, schema migration safety, and fast rollback artifacts available. Always validate with post-upgrade smoke tests and traffic shaping to avoid global impact.
A. Canary upgrade (recommended for minor patch releases):
1. Create a canary deployment with 5-10% of traffic routed (use traffic-split annotation or an ingress rule).
2. Run smoke tests and golden prompt regressions against canary.
3. Monitor key metrics for 30-60 minutes (latency, 5xx rate, gpu OOM).
4. If stable, gradually promote to 25%, 50%, then 100% with validation windows.
5. If regressions appear, terminate canary and rollback to previous image; capture logs and create a regression ticket.

B. Blue/Green (recommended for disruptive upgrades or database migrations):
1. Provision green environment identical to blue (same Helm values with incremented release tag).
2. Run full validation suite in green (smoke + integration tests).
3. Switch traffic at the load balancer (short TTL) to green during a maintenance window.
4. Keep blue environment available for quick rollback for a defined keepalive window (e.g., 30 minutes).
5. If rollback required, re-point traffic to blue and run post-rollback validation.

C. Database & schema migrations (safe path):
- Use backward-compatible migration patterns: add new columns with defaults, two-phase deploy where old and new code can read both schemas.
- Always ship migration scripts separately and make them reversible when possible.
- Schedule migrations in a maintenance window; snapshot DB before migration.

Rollback checklist (immediate actions):
1. Identify failed release and isolate failing components (kubectl -n redwood get pods --selector app=... -o wide).
2. Reduce inbound traffic to the affected release (circuit-breaker or ingress routing).
3. Revert Helm release: helm rollback <release> <revision> --namespace redwood.
4. If helm rollback fails, restore from pre-upgrade snapshot (metadata DB) and redeploy previous bundle.
5. Notify stakeholders, open incident with postmortem owner assigned.

8) Validation & smoke tests (examples)
- Smoke tests include: auth handshake, single-request latency, streaming response correctness, embedding generation and checksum validation, health endpoint checks, and end-to-end sample prompt answer comparison to golden set.
- Example smoke test command: ./smoke-test.sh --endpoint https://redwood-api.local --apikey $API_KEY --tests basic,streaming,embeddings

9) Security & compliance notes
- TLS: mutual TLS for internal control-plane traffic is recommended for multi-tenant customers.
- Audit logs: forward control-plane audit events to customer SIEM; retention per intake form.
- Secrets: use customer KMS or HSM where available; never store plaintext secrets in cluster.
- Hardening: follow CIS Kubernetes benchmarks and run kube-bench pre-deploy.

10) Troubleshooting appendix (common failures & mitigations)
- GPUs not Visible: verify driver + containerd nvidia runtime versions; check node taints/labels and device-plugin logs.
- High p95 latency with low GPU utilization: inspect batching config and model KV cache hit rate; consider increasing batching window for cost-sensitive workloads.
- Post-upgrade 5xx surge: rollback canary/green and examine migration logs for DB timeouts or schema conflicts.

11) Runbooks and links (operational artifacts)
- Core runbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/private-deployments-vpc-onprem-deployment-runbook-2028-03-01
- Packaging & bundle catalog: internal artifact catalog (private link)
- Smoke test repo: git@git.redwood.ai:deployment/smoke-tests.git
- Incident playbooks: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process

Appendix A: Example acceptance criteria checklist (for handover)
- All control-plane endpoints responding to health checks for 24h.
- End-to-end throughput within 10% of expected traffic profile.
- Telemetry ingestion verified and dashboards populated.
- Backups completed and test-restore verified.
- Knowledge transfer and runbook signoff by customer ops.

Appendix B: Contacts & escalation
- Primary oncall (Redwood SRE): sre-oncall@redwood.ai
- Solutions Eng POC: se-ops@redwood.ai
- Product escalation (for bugs affecting multiple customers): product-escalation@redwood.ai

Document maintenance
This guide is maintained by eng-private-deployments. Update cadence: quarterly or on release of a major agent/runtime change. For changes, create a PR to this page and add reviewers from SRE and Solutions Eng.
